Later in the book, Spencer wrote that when Diana first told him she planned to divorce Charles, she claimed that the prince was "in love with his valet."
Spencer said he found the claim improbable but didn't press her for more information because he was focused on the realization that she was ending her marriage and her "dreams."
Princess Diana sits on the steps of Highgrove House.  (Tim Graham Photo Library via Getty Images)

Spencer wrote that his sister had "traditionally feminine" interests, which included collecting numerous stuffed animals as a child. She loved flowers, especially forget-me-nots, listened to the Beatles and David Bowie and liked the soap opera "Crossroads."
As she got older, Spencer wrote, she "devoured" romance novels by Barbara Cartland, whom he said mainly wrote about aristocratic men pursuing virginal women and eventually living happily ever after.

title: Brandi Glanville emptied her 401(k) after spending ‘hundreds of thousands’ on medical bills
summary: Brandi Glanville suffered a concussion, perforated eardrum and cracked rib on "Special Forces" after a helicopter water jump went terribly wrong.
story: Reality star Brandi Glanville explains why her recent financial strain made turning down opportunities more difficult and pushed her to prove she could perform again on FOX's "Special Forces."
Brandi Glanville needed a comeback — personally and financially.
After years of costly health struggles turned her life upside down, the former "Real Housewives of Beverly Hills" star told Fox News Digital she needed to get back to work.

"I had the leisure of saying no in the past, but then I had all these medical bills and whatnot," she admitted. "So I had to say yes. And it was kind of like at a time where I needed to prove to myself that I could do it again."
BRANDI GLANVILLE ENDS UP IN URGENT CARE AFTER TRYING VIRAL TIKTOK TREND

Brandi Glanville revealed that she emptied her 401(k) and spent hundreds of thousands of dollars on medical bills while searching for answers to her debilitating health problems.  (FOX via Getty Images)
But for Glanville, the financial fallout from her health battle has been just as daunting as the physical toll.

"The medical system here is broken," Glanville explained. "So I have, like, from 8 a.m. on, I have creditors from, like, medical things calling me, like from Cedars-Sinai. It's out of control. Like I spent hundreds of thousands of dollars that I had saved. I emptied my 401(k). And it's all for medical bills. And I had insurance, and they told me nothing was wrong. I'm so angry. You know, going into my mid-fifties I had a cushion and that's gone. So it's very scary right now."

After years of suffering, Glanville revealed in September that she had been diagnosed with highly resistant ESBL Klebsiella and Enterobacter with biofilm, coccidioidomycosis, also known as Valley fever, Demodex dermatitis and mononucleosis.
Glanville has said her daily IV treatment was expected to cost between $3,300 and $6,000 per month.
WATCH: BRANDI GLANVILLE SAYS HEALTH BATTLE FORCED HER TO SPEND ‘HUNDREDS OF THOUSANDS'

Brandi Glanville said her ongoing treatment for multiple infections and illnesses is expected to cost between $3,300 and $6,000 per month. (Getty Images/Brandi Glanville/TikTok)

Glanville previously shared that she believed she picked up a parasite after visiting Morocco in 2023. She suffered from facial paralysis and was initially diagnosed with stress-induced angioedema. She told Fox News Digital at the time that she spent more than $70,000 in an attempt to find an answer to the medical mystery that consumed her daily life and disfigured her face.
After everything her body had already endured, Glanville was determined to test her limits on "Special Forces: World's Toughest Test." One challenge pushed those limits further than she expected.

While filming the show, Glanville said contestants were trained on how to fall from a helicopter into the water. But moments before her jump, an instructor told her to keep her head up — a last-second direction she said left her little time to react.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Brandi Glanville also detailed suffering a perforated eardrum, concussion, bruised sternum and cracked rib after hitting the water during a helicopter challenge on "Special Forces." The show airs Thursdays at 9:00 p.m. ET on FOX. (Pete Dadds/FOX)

"My head hit the water. It was like a Mack truck – it, like, ran over my head. I thought that was it," she recalled. "And then a few seconds later, my body hits the water so hard. It was paralyzing almost. I was like, 'Oh my God.' But it was in slow motion."

The former "Real Housewives of Beverly Hills" star said she suffered a perforated eardrum, a concussion, a bruised sternum and a cracked rib — injuries that forced her to travel by boat to the hospital because doctors didn't want her flying. Glanville recalled battling an intense headache on top of the excruciating pain from her rib injury, which made it difficult to breathe or cough.

Brandi Glanville said the painful experience ultimately made her feel proud for pushing herself and completing the challenge. (Tommaso Boddi/Getty Images for Rachel Strauss)

Once at the hospital, Glanville said doctors warned her she couldn't fly and told her she could be stuck there for at least two weeks and potentially need surgery. But after spending several days recovering and returning to the hospital for another evaluation, the reality star said she was determined to leave — even if doctors still weren't thrilled about her getting on a plane.
Battered but undeterred, Glanville said she still considered the experience a personal victory.
"Honestly, I'm so proud of myself. I feel like a badass, even though I didn't last long," she told Fox News Digital. "I went in, I conquered, I got hurt, and then I left and that was enough for me. "

title: Wendi McLendon-Covey fires back after Jeff Garlin blames bipolar disorder for 'The Goldbergs' exit
summary: Jeff Garlin says his undiagnosed bipolar disorder fueled the on-set behavior that led to his exit from "The Goldbergs." Co-star Wendi McLendon-Covey pushed back on his claims.
story: Fox News Flash top entertainment and celebrity headlines are here.

Jeff Garlin is opening up about his contentious exit from "The Goldbergs," saying his undiagnosed bipolar disorder contributed to the behavior that strained relationships with his co-stars before he left the hit sitcom.

The 64-year-old actor starred as the Goldbergs' family patriarch, Murray Goldberg, on the show from its premiere in September 2013 until he departed the ABC show during its ninth season in December 2021 amid HR investigations into complaints about his on-set behavior.

Garlin was accused by members of the cast and crew of inappropriate verbal conduct, unwanted physical contact, including hugging and touching, and behavior that some employees described as creating an uncomfortable work environment.
JEFF GARLIN DEFENDS HIMSELF FROM CANCEL CULTURE AMID ‘THE GOLDBERGS’ ON-SET CONDUCT ALLEGATIONS

While speaking with Vanity Fair at the time, Garlin denied intentionally harassing anyone. He acknowledged that HR had spoken to him over several years but characterized the complaints as stemming from his style of comedy and "silliness" on set rather than malicious intent.
He also said he was willing to adjust behaviors, like no longer hugging people.

Wendi McLendon-Covey is pushing back on her former "The Goldbergs" star Jeff Garlin's claims about his on-set behavior. (Noel Vasquez/Getty Images; Matt Winkelmeyer/Getty Images for International Myeloma Foundation)

During a March 2023 appearance on SiriusXM's "Andy Cohen Live," Garlin's co-star, Wendi McLendon-Covey, who played his wife Beverly Goldberg on "The Goldbergs," said his exit was "a long time coming" and that "finally, someone is listening to us." She declined to discuss the situation further, saying she was "exhausted by that topic and the PTSD of it all."

On Monday, Garlin appeared on the Daily Beast's "Obsessed" podcast and addressed McLendon-Covey's comments and attributed his behavior to a mental health condition that had not been diagnosed at the time.

"It wasn't a long time coming for me," he said in reference to McLendon-Covey's past remark. "I actually empathize with her because, at the time, I was undiagnosed bipolar, and I was miserable on the show.

"I was miserable with my performance," he continued. "She was always trying to tell me, 'Hey, you're really great on the show.' I didn't believe her, and I just got to the point where I had to quit. She was very resentful, and it was a bit dramatic.

"I can only speak to what I'm responsible for," Garlin added. "Being bipolar, I was either one of three things: dark, dark, dark — where I didn't talk or look at anyone — happy to the point of mania, never turning off my thing or mean, really, really mean. I didn't know which one I was going to be. I didn't get diagnosed until I was 59. This was toward the end of my time on ‘The Goldbergs,’ so I could be a lot.
'BLUE BLOODS' STAR JENNIFER ESPOSITO SAYS SHE WAS LOCKED IN PSYCH WARD AS HEALTH BATTLE SPIRALED

"When I left, she was very resentful and angry at me. If she wants to continue the resentment, that's her. I don't have resentment toward her, even for saying things about me. I actually love her, and I appreciate that she's one of the greatest actors I've ever worked with. And that will not be lost on me."
Garlin left the show during its ninth season in 2021. (Disney General Entertainment Content via Getty Images)
McLendon-Covey, 56, responded to Garlin's comments after the Daily Beast shared a clip from his interview on Instagram.
"Huh," she wrote in the comments section.

After an Instagram user asked her, "What’s your take, Wendi?," the "Bridesmaids" star wrote, "Let's just say I remember things very differently, as does the crew, the other actors, the writers and our executives."
Fox News Digital has reached out to representatives for Garlin and McLendon-Covey for comment.
Garlin said his on-set behavior was fueled by undiagnosed bipolar disorder.  (Disney General Entertainment Content via Getty Images)
"The Goldbergs" followed the misadventures of a loud but loving family living in suburban Philadelphia during the 1980s.

Though Garlin left "The Goldbergs" during its ninth season, he was a regular cast member for part of that season. After his exit, the show completed some remaining Season 9 episodes using previously filmed footage and stand-ins before writing Murray Goldberg out ahead of Season 10. At the beginning of the tenth season, the show revealed that the character had died off-screen, allowing the series to continue focusing on the Goldberg family without him.
ABC announced in February 2023 that Season 10 would be the show's last, and the series finale aired on May 3, 2023.

While appearing on the "Obsessed" podcast, Garlin reflected on how his life and career had changed since he was diagnosed with bipolar disorder.
McLendon-Covey disputed his account on social media.  (ABC via Getty Images)

"It's changed quite a bit because, A, I went into AA (Acloholics Anonymous)," he said. "B, I had a nervous breakdown right after that as the ‘The Goldbergs’ thing was ending. I had a nervous breakdown, was suicidal. Went away. Learned this kind of therapy. Got the right drugs in me. The right cocktail, as they say, for bipolar. And I got a form of therapy that was new to me, called Dialectical Behavior Therapy. DBT.

"So, you know, I have regrets," he continued. "Not a lot of them that I could have controlled, but I still have regrets on a lot of my behavior in terms of being a jerk. But I'm really a different person.

"No, I'm the same person," Garlin clarified. "I'm more enlightened.
The two played husband and wife on the hit sitcom.  (Disney General Entertainment Content via Getty Images)

"Like I said, I don't have resentments," he added. "When I have a resentment, I work through it on my own until it doesn't help me any. I'm sober. I'm grateful. I was never grateful for my time on ‘The Goldbergs.’ That was another problem. ‘I’m not grateful for this great opportunity?' No, I wasn't. Because in my heart now, and logically, I know I'm good-hearted, but I wasn't able to — I was misguided. I don't know. But the point is, I'm really grateful for what I have now and the way I am now."

title: Ed Sheeran's Gillette Stadium concerts called off as troubled tour faces fresh setback
summary: Severe weather warnings forced Ed Sheeran's Gillette Stadium shows to be canceled amid a backdrop of controversy involving Macklemore and Robert Kraft.
story: Fox News contributor Raymond Arroyo discusses a fight that broke out on a flight to London and the controversy surrounding Ed Sheeran after Macklemore was dropped from his tour on ‘The Ingraham Angle.’
Ed Sheeran's concerts at Gillette Stadium have been canceled.

Sheeran was set to perform at the Foxborough, Massachusetts, venue on Sept. 25 and 26, but according to a statement shared on social media, potentially dangerous weather conditions have forced the singer to step back.

"Due to the severe weather warnings in place in Boston and across New England throughout the weekend and following consultation with local officials, we have made the difficult decision to cancel the Ed Sheeran concerts at Gillette Stadium," Sheeran's tour promoter, Messina Touring Group, said in a statement. "The decision was made with the safety of fans, staff and everyone involved in the shows as the top priority."
ED SHEERAN CONCERTGOERS WARN ARTISTS ABOUT SHARING POLITICAL VIEWS: 'YOU'RE GOING TO ALIENATE' FANS
Ed Sheeran's shows at Gillette Stadium have been canceled. (Deadline via Getty Images)
The company noted that refunds are available at the point of purchase. Gillette Stadium reposted the statement.

While the weather prompted the cancellations, the owner of Gillette Stadium, Robert Kraft, has been in the headlines recently due to the controversy surrounding Sheeran and one of the former openers for his tour, Macklemore.

After Macklemore used his slot at Sheeran's MetLife Stadium shows to express his support for Palestinians, many people were upset, including owners of stadiums where Sheeran was slated to play. The "Thrift Shop" rapper was eventually dropped from the tour, and in a lengthy statement reacting to the news, he wrote in part, "Ed also told me that Kraft had rallied some of the other stadium owners and collectively they gave him an ultimatum: if Macklemore stays on the tour, you will not be allowed to play in our venues."
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Macklemore was dropped from Sheeran's tour after using his set to speak about his political views. (Redferns)

Kraft then issued a statement of his own that read, "Gillette Stadium has a longstanding commitment to providing a welcoming environment for all guests and ensuring that events held at our venue do not provide a platform for hate speech."

"Based on Macklemore’s recent actions, material shared from the stage during Ed Sheeran’s shows in New Jersey, and a broader history of antisemitic rhetoric and imagery that we believe has been deeply offensive and hurtful to the Jewish community, we determined that his participation in the September 25th and 26th concerts at Gillette Stadium would cross that line."

The statement continued, "This decision is not about diminishing the suffering of innocent Palestinians or denying anyone the right to advocate on their behalf. Their pain and loss are real. But that advocacy should not come at the expense of the Jewish community or obscure the responsibility of Hamas, a United States and globally (including Canada, European Union, United Kingdom, and Japan) designated terrorist organization whose horrific actions have caused immeasurable suffering for Palestinians and Israelis alike."
Robert Kraft, owner of Gillette Stadium, has said that he's a fan of Sheeran. (Kara Durrette/Getty Images)

Kraft wrote that he agreed with Macklemore that "too many lives have been lost and there has been too much suffering," but argued that "only sharing selective information and ignoring the actions of Hamas is not honest and only advances more divisiveness and hate."
He added, "Standing with the Palestinian people and standing against Hamas, antisemitism and hate should not be mutually exclusive."

Kraft shared that he's spent a considerable amount of time in recent years "focused on the fight against antisemitism and hate of all kinds, and I feel a responsibility to stand up when I believe that line has been crossed."

He has a "tremendous respect" for Sheeran and his music, Kraft explained, and he said that he'd also be happy to speak personally with Macklemore, "because ultimately our goal is the same – peace for all people, an end to suffering, and an end to all hate."

While it's not clear if Macklemore has pursued that opportunity, he did announce this week that in October, he's headed to Europe for a set of shows he's calling the "Free Palestine Tour."
Despite the promoter saying severe weather forced the cancellation of Sheeran's Gillette Stadium shows, several people shared other theories on social media.
"Mother Nature really said ‘not in Kraft’s house,'" one person wrote.
Sheeran's opening acts have backed out of the tour following Macklemore's exit. (Kevin Mazur/Getty Images for iHeartRadio)

story: Tiffany Darwish told Fox News Digital that by 6 PM everyday, she is in the kitchen cooking before a peaceful night.
'80s pop icon Tiffany is stepping back into the spotlight as she fulfills a dream she had prior to becoming a teen idol.
The 54-year-old singer, who rose to fame in 1987 after her song "I Think We're Alone Now" became a massive hit, made her Off-Broadway debut in "Spandex the Musical" last week.
During a July interview with People magazine, Tiffany reflected on why taking the stage felt like a "true full-circle moment for me."
'80S POP STAR TIFFANY EMBRACES QUIET NASHVILLE ROUTINE AFTER LEAVING CALIFORNIA BEHIND FOR GOOD
"Before music came into my life, I was a dancer and an actor, and those dreams were put on hold when ‘I Think We’re Alone Now’ took off and my recording career began," she said.
'80s icon Tiffany is stepping back into the spotlight to fulfill her lifelong dream after leaving Hollywood. (Bruce Glikas/Getty Images; Frank Hempel/United Archives via Getty Images)

Tiffany, whose full name is Tiffany Darwish, launched her career with the now-legendary Shopping Mall Tour '87, performing free concerts at malls across the country beginning in June 1987. The grassroots campaign helped turn the then-15-year-old into a teen sensation before she became a chart-topping artist.

In September 1987, Tiffany's cover of Tommy James and the Shondells' 1967 hit "I Think We're Alone Now" climbed to No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 less than two months after its release and made her a household name.

"I Think We're Alone Now" was the second single released from her self-titled debut album. She followed up with "Could've Been," the third single released from "Tiffany," which also topped the Billboard Hot 100. In addition, the album produced her Beatles cover "I Saw Him Standing There," which peaked at No. 7 on the Billboard Hot 100, and "Feelings of Forever," which reached the No. 50 spot.
Tiffany rose to fame at 15 with her hit song "I Think We're Alone Now." (Ron Eisenberg/Michael Ochs Archives/Getty Images)

At 16, Tiffany became the youngest female artist to top the Billboard 200 with a debut album. She went on to headline her first major tour in 1988, with New Kids on the Block opening for her before the boy band's own meteoric rise.

However, Tiffany's chart dominance proved difficult to sustain. While her 1988 sophomore album, "Hold an Old Friend's Hand," was certified platinum by the RIAA and produced the Top 10 hit "All This Time," it fell short of matching the success of her debut. As the teen-pop landscape shifted in the early 1990s, her third album, "New Inside," failed to gain commercial traction.
RICK MORANIS, CAMERON DIAZ AND LINDSAY LOHAN AMONG STARS WHO LEFT FAME BEHIND BEFORE RETURNING TO HOLLYWOOD

In 1993, Tiffany released her fourth album, "Dreams Never Die," which was issued only in Asian markets. Afterward, Tiffany largely stepped back from the mainstream music scene to focus on raising her son Elijah, whom she shares with her ex-husband, makeup artist Bulmaro Garcia. The two were married from 1992 to 2003.
In the early 2000s, Tiffany left Hollywood behind and moved to Nashville. During a 2023 interview with Fox News Digital, she explained why she decided to embrace a simpler life in Tennessee.
She became the youngest female artist to have an album top the Billboard 200. (Paul Massey/Mirrorpix/Getty Images)
DOLLY PARTON'S PATH FROM NASHVILLE NEWCOMER TO BILLBOARD'S NO. 1 COUNTRY MUSIC ARTIST OF ALL TIME

"I came to Nashville for the first time when I was 10," the California native recalled. "I’ve been coming back ever since. I love being out in the country – I’m a country girl at heart. I’ve toured all over the world and this place has always been home for me. There’s just something about coming home to my little ranch… I’ve never looked back."

Since the days of her teenage stardom, Tiffany has continued to tour and release music as an independent artist. She has also made appearances in movies and television shows and starred in several reality TV series.

During a June interview with Fox News Digital, Tiffany detailed how she spent the past several years building a culinary brand that combines her love of cooking, entertaining and connecting with fans. Through her platform, "Let's Food With Tiffany," she offers recipes, virtual cooking experiences and food-focused events that showcase the same energy and creativity that made her a pop sensation.

Earlier this year, Tiffany released her second cookbook, "POP LIFE: The Ultimate ‘80s Kitchen Encore," which she created with Las Vegas celebrity chef Alicia Shevetone. "POP LIFE: The Ultimate ’80s Kitchen Encore" followed her first cookbook, "Breakfast with Tiffany," which she released independently.
Tiffany left Hollywood for Nashville in the early 2000s. (Lorne Thomson /Darlene Hammond)

In July, Tiffany announced that she would make her New York theatrical debut in "Spandex the Musical," in which she plays Linda Gustafson, a housewife who competes in the fictional 1988 Crystal Light National Aerobics Championship.
"I’ve always believed the right role would find me, and the moment I read the script, I knew Linda was that character," she told People magazine at the time.

"Just as Linda discovers a new passion through aerobics that changes her life, I’ve found exciting new passions beyond music through my ‘Pop Life’ cookbook, ‘Let’s Food With Tiffany’ events, and now returning to acting on stage," she continued. "It’s a reminder that it’s never too late to reinvent yourself."

"Spandex: The Musical" is a 10-day limited Off-Broadway engagement which runs through Sept. 27. After each performance, Tiffany performs "I Think We're Alone Now" during the curtain call.
She is currently starring in Off-Broadway's "Spandex: The Musical." (Bruce Glikas/Getty Images)

"There are so many wonderful parallels between Linda’s journey and my own, and I’m thrilled the producers have even woven in some fun Tiffany Easter eggs that I know longtime fans are going to love," she told People.

Tiffany said the project is especially meaningful because a portion of the show's proceeds will benefit Children's Miracle Network, a nonprofit organization that raises money for 170 children's hospitals across the United States and Canada.

title: Meghan Markle’s outing with Ellen DeGeneres exposes 'irony' in royal’s ‘quiet country life’: expert
summary: Meghan Markle's first photographed outing in the Cotswolds with Ellen DeGeneres and Portia de Rossi raises questions about her quiet life claims.
story: Kinsey Schofield, host of YouTube's "Kinsey Schofield Unfiltered," argues Prince Harry and Meghan Markle choose publicity while seeking privacy and says their royal status should be made clear.
Meghan Markle is raising questions after being photographed in England with two Hollywood stars.

The 45-year-old royal was recently photographed in the Cotswolds with Ellen DeGeneres and her wife, Portia de Rossi, in her first photographed outing since arriving in the U.K., which Kinsey Schofield, host of YouTube’s "Kinsey Schofield Unfiltered" said hints that "there is already going to be considerably less privacy for Meghan in Britain than perhaps she anticipated."

"But there is an irony here too. If Harry and Meghan genuinely wanted to disappear into quiet country life, the Cotswolds is one of the places where they could probably accomplish that," Schofield told Fox News Digital. "Instead, Meghan’s first photographed social outing is with Ellen DeGeneres and Portia de Rossi. That tells me she remains very interested in celebrity and in being associated with recognizable, high-profile people."

Schofield added that she finds it "interesting" that Markle "appears to have changed countries without necessarily changing the social ecosystem she prefers," noting that when living in Montecito, she and Prince Harry were spending time with "wealthy, famous and influential people."
Markle was photographed with Ellen DeGeneres and Portia de Rossi in her first public outing since moving back to England. (Harold Cunningham/Getty Images)
PRINCE HARRY, MEGHAN MARKLE ACCUSED OF SEEKING ‘BEST OF BOTH WORLDS’ WITH UK MOVE: EXPERT

The idea that her first photographed outing since moving to the U.K. was with "two fellow American celebrity transplants" isn't "inherently wrong" in Schofield's eyes, but she argues that it challenges the "idea that Meghan has returned to Britain simply to embrace a quieter, more anonymous country life."
"If anything, this suggests she may be trying to recreate elements of Montecito in the Cotswolds: privacy when she wants it, but with a glamorous and recognizable social circle around her," she said.

"She’s saying ‘I’m a Hollywood celebrity’ rather than a royal and am thus far 'sticking to celebrity lane insulated by privilege and not integrating into English life,'" Fordwich said.
Schofield, however, questioned Markle's decision to have DeGeneres be the first celebrity she was photographed with, as "it inevitably resurrects an uncomfortable conversation for her."

"Ellen’s reputation was badly damaged by allegations about the workplace culture surrounding her show, while Meghan herself has faced serious allegations about her treatment of Palace staff, which she has strongly denied," Schofield said. "Given that history, I am surprised Meghan would want photographs of the two of them together circulating so soon after her return to Britain. It invites comparisons I would imagine her advisers would rather avoid."

Schofield explained that Prince Harry is more interested in portraying the life of a working royal, despite not being one. (WireImage/Getty Images)

Schofield also noted that Markle's behavior, in comparison to Prince Harry's, also highlights her interest "in commercial and monetary opportunities," while showing he is "determined to maintain the appearance and rhythm of royal life."

"Harry likes the engagements, the causes, the speeches and the sense of public duty," she said. "Meghan seems happier pursuing celebrity and commercial opportunities. So I don’t necessarily think her absence from Harry’s events is accidental. They may simply have very different ideas about what they want their lives back in Britain to look like."

title: Ed Sheeran concertgoers warn artists about sharing political views: 'You're going to alienate' fans
summary: Ed Sheeran fans at his Philadelphia concert warned artists that political statements alienate audiences. Sheeran's Gillette Stadium shows, planned for the weekend, were canceled due to weather.
story: The "Shape of You" singer held a solo concert last weekend in Philadelphia after Macklemore was dropped from the tour over his pro-Palestinian comments.

Several fans who attended Ed Sheeran’s concert in Philadelphia last weekend after Macklemore was dropped for making "Free Palestine" comments, warned other artists that if they make political statements, they will alienate half of their audience.

The "Bad Habits" singer was expected to play his second and third concerts since the controversy this Friday and Saturday at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts, which is owned by Robert Kraft.
However, both shows have since been canceled.

"Due to the severe weather warnings in place in Boston and across New England throughout the weekend and following consultation with local officials, we have made the difficult decision to cancel the Ed Sheeran concerts at Gillette Stadium," tour promoter Messina Touring said in a statement on Friday. "The decision was made with the safety of fans, staff and everyone involved in the shows as the top priority."
ROBERT KRAFT, GILLETTE STADIUM BOOT MACKLEMORE FROM ED SHEERAN TOUR OVER ‘FREE PALESTINE’ RANT
Ed Sheeran is seen performing at a concert in December. (Kevin Mazur/Getty Images for iHeartRadio)
Previously, the New England Patriots owner allegedly threatened to cancel the concerts at his venue if Macklemore wasn’t taken off the tour, according to the "Thrift Shop" rapper.
Macklemore also claimed Kraft got other stadium owners to agree to not allow Sheeran to play at their venues if the rapper was still with his tour.

"The fact that they’re forcing Ed Sheeran to have an opinion is not right," one woman told Fox News Digital outside last Saturday’s concert. "He wants to stay in the middle – if you have an opinion, that’s fine, but you’re going to alienate at least 50% of your population, and it causes unrest."
GOO GOO DOLLS' JOHN RZEZNIK DRAWS LINE ON POLITICS AT CONCERTS: 'I'M NOT GOING TO LECTURE YOU'

She said the "Shape of You" singer "just wants to do his music and play his music, and people want to enjoy it. They want to get away from it, and I don’t feel as though they should have to worry about this stuff when they come to a concert."

Macklemore was dropped as the opening act for Sheeran’s tour earlier this month after he made pro-Palestinian comments at two concerts. The other supporting acts on Sheeran’s tour quit in solidarity with Macklemore.
WATCH: ED SHEERAN CONCERTGOERS WEIGH IN ON MUSICIANS MAKING POLITICAL STATEMENTS
LIBERAL LAWMAKERS, ACTIVISTS RALLY BEHIND MACKLEMORE AFTER SHEERAN TOUR REMOVAL OVER 'FREE PALESTINE' STANCE

In Philadelphia Saturday night, Sheeran made a nearly four-minute-long speech in which he explained to fans that he never wanted to be an activist musician and that he was there continuing his tour alone because he wanted to honor his commitment to fans.
Macklemore performs at a concert at the end of August. (AFP via Getty Images)
ED SHEERAN FACES GROWING BACKLASH AS RADIO STATION BANS SONGS, PROTEST GROUPS RESPOND TO MACKLEMORE'S REMOVAL
He said he can also see both sides of such a complex issue, admitting that he doesn’t know enough about it, is still learning and will make mistakes as he tries to navigate the situation.

He added that he could no longer hide how he feels about the humanitarian issue.

Another fan told Fox News Digital ahead of the concert last Saturday that, as artists and musicians have a right to speak their minds: "They also don’t have to — they’re entertainment. I have a right to choose to listen or to not listen. I think it’s all about my choice — I live in America, I can decide to ignore or to listen, and they have the same right."
Fans arrive for Ed Sheeran's concert at Lincoln Financial Field in Philadelphia on Sept. 19. (AFP via Getty Images)
GORILLAZ FRONTMAN DAMON ALBARN HOLDS UP PALESTINIAN FLAG DURING SHOW AFTER MACKLEMORE TOUR REMOVAL

"It’s a really tough thing," a woman, who told Fox News Digital she is a schoolteacher, said outside the concert. "I am in a classroom every day, and I have my own thoughts on politics in the same way that I’m sure every artist does. I also do not share those with my students because I want them to have a safe space where they are who they are, and I think that’s kind of the same way I want concerts to be. I want us to have a space where we can be happy and get away from the rest of the world for a little while, and that’s why we’re here."

Demonstrators protest outside Ed Sheeran's concert in Philadelphia on Sept. 19. (Getty Images)

We all come from different backgrounds, different understandings, and trying to group all those together and say, ‘You only have to have one opinion of everything,’ I think it kind of makes it rough for everyone to kind of just enjoy their lives and enjoy what makes them happy."

Patriots owner Robert Kraft also owns Gillette Stadium, where Ed Sheeran was set to play two concerts this weekend. The shows were canceled due to weather. (Bryan Bennett/Getty Images)
Another woman at the concert noted that musicians like Sheeran are just trying to make a living.

"I support the artists — they’re here for the right reasons, and they’re here to make a living, they’re doing something that they love, and they pursue their music for a reason," she told Fox News Digital. "We enjoy his music and that’s what we’re here for, minus everything else, we’re just here for a good time."

title: Sydney Sweeney gives subtle nod to boyfriend Scooter Braun in new lingerie campaign
summary: Sydney Sweeney's new Syrn lingerie campaign features a delicate gold "SB" necklace that appears to be a subtle nod to boyfriend Scooter Braun.
story: Make America Hot Again founder Raquel Debono slams left-wing media and influencers after intense backlash to Sydney Sweeney's bare-all Novig ad.

In photos shared by the company, Sweeney modeled a pale pink bra from the brand while wearing the gold necklace, with the two small letters visible around her neck.

The company explained that the new design uses the same fit as its Romantic Demi bra but features a smooth cup intended to be worn under T-shirts.

title: Country music star Ella Langley faces her fears following record-breaking week
summary: A TikTok video shows Ella Langley holding an Argentine boa, a parrot, a baby kangaroo and a lemur during her wild exotic animal adventure day.
story: Ella Langley speaks about her deep appreciation for supporters and how their connection transformed her path while attending the 2026 iHeartRadio Music Awards.
Ella Langley is choosin' to face her fears this week.

On Wednesday, the country music star shared a TikTok video of herself meeting and holding several exotic animals. Langley had a parrot on her shoulder and sat next to a baby kangaroo on a couch before she decided to take it to the next level.
"This is facing my fears a little bit," the singer said when she was presented with an Argentine boa.
ELLA LANGLEY SAYS 'CHOOSIN' TEXAS' SUCCESS IS 'CHANGING MY LIFE' AFTER HER SONG BREAKS MARIAH CAREY'S RECORD
Ella Langley faced her fears and held an Argentine Boa in a TikTok video. (Ella Langley/TikTok; Getty Images)
Langley appeared to be a little nervous when she first held the snake but eventually warmed up to it. She allowed the boa constrictor to wrap around her shoulders and rest on her body.
The TikTok video ended with Langley hugging and holding a lemur.
"I love today," she said.
The comment section was filled with fans weighing in on Langley's exotic animal experience.
"So fun!" one user wrote. Another added, "omg the snakes I would have ran."

Ella Langley has become one of country music's fastest rising stars. (Jason Kempin/Getty Images)

title: Roseanne Barr calls former co-star a 'brainwashed bigot' after he said reboot was 'rightfully canceled'
summary: Roseanne Barr called Michael Fishman a "brainwashed bigot" on a podcast after he said the 2018 "Roseanne" hit reboot was "rightfully canceled."
story: Roseanne Barr told Fox News Digital she believes her upbringing was the perfect depiction of the American experience.
Roseanne Barr is firing back at her former co-star, calling him a "brainwashed bigot."

During a recent appearance on the "Can't Be Censored" podcast, the 73-year-old actress and comedian hit back at her former "Roseanne" co-star, Michael Fishman, after he said the 2018 reboot was "rightfully canceled."

"He f---ing doesn’t even f---ing know what I said, even though I’ve explained it 10,000 times for nine years on the internet," Barr said. "He hasn’t even taken the time to listen to what I say because he’s a bigot. And he’s a brainwashed bigot."

The reboot of the hit '90s show was a huge success when it premiered in March 2018 but was canceled just two months later after Barr tweeted a racist remark about Valerie Jarrett, a former advisor to former President Obama.
Barr fired back at her former co-star who said ABC was right to cancel the "Roseanne" reboot. (Getty Images)
ROSEANNE BARR REVEALS ‘DAMAGED’ HEART, FEARS SHE WILL ‘DIE ON THE SURGERY TABLE’

Barr apologized for the remark multiple times. However, ABC decided to fire her and cancel the show. A month later, the network announced a new spin-off called "The Connors," bringing back a majority of the "Roseanne" cast without any involvement from Barr.
The comedian went on to say that Fishman asked her about her comments "9,000" times before she told him to "go and f--- yourself and stay f---ed ‘till the day you die."

"Don’t put my name in your f---ng mouth; shut the f--- up," she recalled telling him. "You are an ignoramus and a bigot, and you have no idea what I said because it contradicts the Democratic Party platform that you’ve had shoved down your throat and up your a--. So, just f--- you. You have no geopolitical context whatsoever to discuss what I said."
Fishman fired back after Barr reignited their years-old feud, but the former child star appeared to take a different approach to the comedian’s blistering comments.

"I know everybody wants a response to Roseanne’s comments," Fishman said in a statement shared on social media, before taking a moment to thank Barr for acknowledging that he did reach out to her after her 2018 controversy.
Michael Fishman and Roseanne Barr appear in a 1990 episode of "Roseanne." (ABC Photo Archives / Getty Images)

Fishman continued to explain that he showed Barr "compassion" during her scandal, even though he "vehemently disagreed" with her. He said that her memory of how she responded to his attempts to discuss the issue was accurate, and that he'd kept the things she said to him to himself "for her protection."

"But I guess she gave you a glimpse into the darker side of my childhood," he admitted, before adding that he does have "tremendous gratitude" for the time he spent working with her on the original show.

The actor, who played D.J. Conner on "Roseanne," also reflected on the complicated nature of their relationship, saying, "I’m living something publicly that a lot of you have been navigating privately," referring to the experience of "caring and loving someone who’s been a powerful part of your life and who’s changed and we don’t understand. And we don’t agree with it."

Despite the fallout, Fishman said he plans to respond with compassion rather than anger. "I’m going to choose to remember the best in them, and I’m also going to set some healthy boundaries for myself," he said. "We get to decide who we are, and our actions show who we are." He concluded his statement by saying, "I’m going to make art from the joy and the pain."
Metcalf said she hasn't spoken to Barr since they finished filming the reboot. (Adam Rose/Disney General Entertainment Content via Getty Images)
In a recent interview with The New Yorker, Laurie Metcalf, who played Barr's sister, Jackie Harris, on the show, said the two "haven’t spoken since we said goodbye at the end of the reboot."
Barr confirmed she has not kept in touch with any of her former co-stars during an interview with Fox News Digital in June 2025.

"No, I'm not friends with none of them. They're all in the past," she said. "I have pleasant memories of what fun we had, wish them all the best. And, no, we don't talk. I've moved on from that horrendous ending and chapter of my life, but you know, I don't hold any bitterness or nothing to them. But, my God, what fun we had on that show.

title: Dolly Parton’s sisters push back on feud rumors after nephew’s legal battle with star's estate erupts

Macklemore is taking his views on "Free Palestine" on the road.

The rapper, who was dropped from Ed Sheeran's tour earlier this month after stirring controversy with his politically charged performances, announced Thursday that he's going on a new tour he's calling the "Free Palestine Tour."

"If these last couple of weeks have shown us anything, it’s that something has shifted over the last three years. Macklemore wrote that "what happened to me is bigger than one artist or one stage," and that "when the billionaire class can decide which voices are allowed on stage and which ones are too dangerous to hear, everyone should be paying attention."
He added, "So, as you all know, my schedule freed up a bit."

title: Scientists reveal surprisingly easy exercise that may boost your mood in just 10 minutes
summary: A University of Tsukuba study found that a slow 10-minute jog boosted attention, self-control and mood in young adults by activating the prefrontal cortex.
story: A University of Tsukuba study indicates that running at very slow speed can enhance mood and cognitive function. Dr. Jessica Gray, a family medicine physician, joins 'Fox & Friends First' to discuss the details.
It might not take an all-out sprint or long trail run to lift your mood and sharpen focus, according to a new study.
A new study from the University of Tsukuba in Japan looked at 24 healthy young adults who completed a slow, 10-minute run on a treadmill in one session and rested in another.

After the easy jog, participants performed faster on a test of attention and self-control and reported feeling more alert and pleasant than they did after the resting phase, according to the small study published in the journal Imaging Neuroscience in August.
'PERFECT' WORKOUT FORMULA CAN TAKE JUST 10 MINUTES A DAY, HILARIA BALDWIN SAYS
Brain monitoring after the jog also showed more activity in parts of the prefrontal cortex, the area of the brain responsible for focus and decision-making.
The jog was purposely kept easy, with participants going at speeds from 1.9 to 3.7 mph on the treadmill. Their average heart rates clocked in at 105 to 107 beats per minute.
A small study suggests even a brief, easy jog may offer a short-term boost in mood and focus. (iStock)
"A single bout of running, even at very slow speed, elicits a pleasant mood and improved executive function," the researchers found.
SIMPLE BODY MOVEMENT COULD HELP THE BRAIN 'CLEAN ITSELF,' RESEARCHERS FIND
The finding "sheds light on the slow running benefits to brain health," they added.
Even gentle movement can provide a mental reset, though the study’s findings were limited to one short session. (iStock)
The benefits, they noted, stuck around even after participants' heart rates returned to baseline.
JUST 10 MINUTES OF DAILY FLOOR EXERCISES MAY IMPROVE BALANCE AND AGILITY, STUDY FINDS
The greater the up-and-down head movement during the jog, the more positive the participants' mood was afterward, though that finding was exploratory and does not necessarily prove cause and effect.
5 COMMON WALKING MISTAKES THAT COULD HURT YOUR PROGRESS, ACCORDING TO AN EXPERT

"Easy movement triggers the norepinephrine and dopamine pathways that wake up the part of the brain that is in charge of focus and self-control," said Dr. John La Puma, a California-based internist and author of "Indoor Epidemic," who was not involved in the study.
Brain monitoring during the post-jog attention test showed greater activity in prefrontal regions involved in focus and decision-making. (iStock)
Experts agree, however, that it does not mean one brief workout could be a cure-all.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

"A brief jog should help someone get some energy in their system, which may make them feel better about themselves mentally and help them focus," said Dr. Scott Nass, a California-based family medicine physician at SwiftCareMD.
But Nass, who also wasn't involved in the research, said the effect is likely temporary.
Participants completed a test measuring attention and self-control after a 10-minute easy jog and after a resting session. (iStock)
For people living with depression or anxiety, a jog may briefly clear the mind but is "no substitute for medical care," he told Fox News Digital.

The study was also limited in that it included just 24 healthy, young adults and measured outcomes immediately after just one exercise session.
The findings cannot be assumed to apply to older adults, novice runners or people with health conditions, and larger studies are necessary to confirm the results, Nass said.

For a practical approach, La Puma suggested taking a 10-minute walk outside before the most mentally demanding part of the day.
Add 30-second jogging intervals, keeping the pace easy enough to speak in full sentences without becoming breathless, he said.
After the slow jog, participants reported feeling more alert and pleasant than they did after the resting session. (iStock)
People with heart disease, high blood pressure, Type 1 diabetes, recent surgery or joint pain should check with a clinician before starting a new routine, La Puma advised.

title: Doctor reveals '10-year rule' for evaluating brain fog and dementia symptoms
summary: A UCLA neurology professor's 10-year self-assessment helps women determine if memory loss stems from estrogen changes during perimenopause or dementia.
story: Dr. Rhonda Voskuhl discusses how declining estrogen may affect cognitive function and why healthy lifestyle habits may not address every menopause-related change.

Losing a train of thought, struggling to recall once-familiar words or forgetting the reason for walking into a room can leave older adults wondering if they are experiencing early signs of Alzheimer’s disease or dementia.

However, these brain blips can often be tied to hormone shifts later in life, medical experts note, and women who experience a loss of estrogen during perimenopause and menopause are particularly affected.

According to Dr. Rhonda Voskuhl, a professor of neurology at UCLA and co-founder of Cleopatra RX in Los Angeles, women experiencing memory struggles in midlife should compare their cognitive function to their own past performance before assuming something is seriously wrong.
WOMEN WHO START COMMON HORMONE THERAPY IN THEIR 50S MAY HAVE 23% LOWER DEMENTIA RISK
"I think they should listen to themselves," Voskuhl told Fox News Digital at the Livelong Women’s Health Summit in New York City Friday. "They know. Just ask yourself."
For women, sudden memory lapses in midlife are often driven by estrogen loss during perimenopause and menopause rather than early-onset dementia. (iStock)
The 10-year assessment
To help women gauge whether their memory lapses are tied to hormonal shifts, Voskuhl recommends using a quick benchmark of comparing a current mental state to where it was a decade ago.
"The first question is, are you worse than you were 10 years ago?" she said, referencing the Voskuhl Brain Fog Menopause Assessment used at UCLA's Comprehensive Menopausal Program.
KATIE COURIC COULDN'T REMEMBER THE YEAR OR THE PRESIDENT DURING FRIGHTENING BRAIN EPISODE

"Ten years is a pretty good spot. And they think, ‘What was I doing 10 years ago? What was I like? Was I having problems finding the words? Was I at the point where I couldn’t multitask anymore? Was I slow in my processing?’ And they’ll remember."
This comparison can help reveal whether a woman’s cognitive changes may be linked to menopause, while giving patients and physicians a baseline for tracking symptoms over time.
CDC data shows that about one in nine adults report subjective cognitive decline, but less than half ever discuss these memory concerns with a healthcare professional. (iStock)
The NFL analogy

Standard memory tests don’t always catch subtle shifts in everyday cognitive function. In the medical community, this is known as subjective cognitive decline, when patients notice changes even though neurological testing remains normal.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reports that roughly one in nine adults report subjective cognitive decline, yet less than half discuss these memory concerns with a healthcare professional.
To illustrate why routine tests can miss early menopausal brain fog, Voskuhl compared it to a high-performing athlete.
"They know if they're not like they used to be."
"If somebody is an NFL football player, and he says, 'I'm weaker than I used to be,' and I go and do my neurological test, I say, 'Oh no, you're still strong,'" Voskuhl said.
What the player is feeling still matters, even if a standard test shows no obvious decline, she noted.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Women, too, can often recognize when their cognitive abilities have changed from their own baseline and should trust those observations, according to Voskuhl.

Standard neurological tests frequently miss menopausal brain fog because patients experience "subjective cognitive decline," noticing subtle personal drops in performance that clinical tests register as normal. (iStock)
Understanding the difference between hormonal brain fog and neurodegenerative disease comes down to how memory loss impacts daily function, experts agree.

Menopausal brain fog typically involves temporary, inconsistent lapses like misplacing items or experiencing slower processing speed, but overall reasoning skills and independence remain intact, according to the Mayo Clinic. Symptoms often fluctuate and can be exacerbated by stress or poor sleep.

By contrast, early dementia causes persistent, progressive memory loss that interferes with basic daily tasks like managing finances, following familiar routes while driving or exercising sound judgment.
If cognitive concerns arise, experts advise getting a thorough medical evaluation to rule out other issues and finding a new doctor if symptoms are being dismissed. (iStock)
Amid cognitive concerns, experts advise seeking a full medical evaluation, including brain MRIs or vascular screenings, to rule out underlying issues like blood vessel disease or thyroid imbalances.

title: Never smoked a cigarette? You could still be at higher risk for lung cancer
summary: Never-smokers carrying the rare EGFR T790M gene variant face 62 times the odds of lung cancer, a major study of 3.3 million people suggests.
story: Fox News senior medical analyst Dr. Marc Siegel discusses a new study revealing a historic decline in adult cigarette smoking rates in the U.S. to under 10%.
A rare genetic mutation could put people at a dramatically higher risk of developing lung cancer even if they’ve never smoked.

A rare mutation in the gene EGFR T790M was found to increase lung cancer risk by 25 times compared with people who did not have the mutation, according to a new study published in the journal Science.
Among people who had never smoked, carriers of the mutation had about 62 times the odds of lung cancer compared with never-smokers who did not have it.
PANCREATIC CANCER VACCINE SHOWS PROMISE IN FIRST HUMAN TRIAL, PREVENTING DISEASE IN HIGH-RISK PATIENTS
The study, led by investigators at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute and 23andMe Research Institute, analyzed data from more than 3.3 million people.
The gene variant showed no increased risk across 17 other cancers studied.
A rare genetic mutation could put people at a dramatically higher risk of developing lung cancer even if they’ve never smoked. (iStock)

"Today, lung cancer screening is driven almost entirely by smoking history," study co-author Jaclyn LoPiccolo, attending physician and lung cancer researcher at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, said in a press release.
CANCER WARNING SIGNS MAY APPEAR IN DNA YEARS BEFORE BLOOD TESTS DETECT TROUBLE

"Our findings raise the possibility that, in the future, screening could also be dictated by inherited genetic risk. If further studies confirm the benefit, people with EGFR T790M could be identified through genetic testing and offered personalized CT screening to identify lung cancers when they are at their most curable stage."
Among people who had never smoked, carriers of the mutation had about 62 times the odds of lung cancer compared with never-smokers who did not have it. (iStock)
Most U.S. carriers of the mutation were traced to a shared ancestry linked to British and Irish settlers in Southern Appalachia about 200–225 years ago, the researchers found.

The mutation remains rare nationwide, affecting roughly one in 15,000–16,000 people. It is more common in some parts of Southern Appalachia, where researchers estimate as many as one in 2,000 people may carry it.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"We found that the vast majority of carriers inherited the mutation from the same ancestral lineage," said LoPiccolo. "We could trace that lineage to British and Irish settlers in the United States and show that the mutation became enriched after a founder event and genetic bottleneck in Southern Appalachia about 200 years ago.
"It's a fascinating example of how human migration and genealogy can shape disease risk, generations later."
While the study establishes a strong association with lung cancer risk, it does not demonstrate that genetic testing improves mortality or other health outcomes. (iStock)
One of the "remarkable" findings of the study was the fact that a single mutation could have such a strong effect, according to Alexander Gusev, a quantitative geneticist at Dana-Farber.
"To my knowledge, it's one of the strongest, if not the strongest, cancer risk-increasing mutations that has ever been found," he said in the release.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"Smoking is bad for lung cancer. This mutation is bad for lung cancer. When you do both, your risk is the sum of those two risks," he added. "So, you definitely don't want to smoke."

The researchers suggest that people with a strong family history of lung cancer, multiple lung nodules or tumors or family roots in parts of the southeastern U.S. should consider speaking with a genetic counselor about whether genetic testing or lung cancer screening makes sense for them.
"It's a fascinating example of how human migration and genealogy can shape disease risk generations later."
There were some limitations to the study.
Because the mutation is so rare, researchers identified relatively few carriers even among the millions of participants, meaning the exact size of the increased risk remains uncertain.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
The analysis also relied heavily on 23andMe research participants, who may not represent the broader population.
Because the mutation is much more common in certain parts of the U.S., the risk estimates may not apply equally to everyone, the researchers noted.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
While the study establishes a strong association with lung cancer risk, it does not demonstrate that genetic testing improves mortality or other health outcomes.
The study was funded in part by the National Institutes of Health and the American Cancer Society.

title: Popular weight-loss drugs may play surprising role in cancer outcomes
summary: GLP-1 drugs like Ozempic and Wegovy may lower cancer risk by altering the body's immune response, but researchers say key clinical trials are needed.
story: Sai Yendamuri, M.D., a thoracic surgeon at Roswell Park Comprehensive Cancer Center in Buffalo, New York, speaks to Fox News Digital about whether weight-loss drugs could reduce cancer risk.
As GLP-1 medications continue reshaping the treatment of obesity and diabetes, researchers are also investigating whether the drugs could influence cancer risk and outcomes.
The American Association for Cancer Research's 2026 Cancer Progress Report, released earlier this month, noted that obesity is a major risk factor for many cancers.

As glucagon-like peptide-1 medications – including semaglutides like Ozempic and Wegovy, and tirzepatides like Mounjaro and Zepbound – are known to cause substantial weight loss and improve metabolic health, they have attracted significant interest among cancer researchers.
POPULAR WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS MAY HELP PROTECT AGAINST A DEADLY DISEASE, DOCTOR SAYS
While the AACR report cited studies suggesting GLP-1 medications may reduce the risk of certain cancers, it emphasized that the overall evidence is mixed and more research is needed.
"Randomized clinical trials remain the gold standard ... however, such trials have not yet been conducted specifically to assess cancer outcomes associated with GLP-1 RA use," the report stated.
As GLP-1 medications continue reshaping the treatment of obesity and diabetes, researchers are also investigating whether the drugs could influence cancer risk and outcomes. (iStock)

Sai Yendamuri, M.D., a thoracic surgeon at Roswell Park Comprehensive Cancer Center in Buffalo, New York, reiterated that obesity is a leading cause of cancer, second to smoking. Additional risk factors include alcohol and poor nutrition, he noted, "which are all layered into obesity."

"So if obesity is related to cancer – both in terms of causing it and increasing its progression – the logical question is, would a drug that decreases obesity have an impact?" the doctor, who was not associated with the AACR report, said in an interview with Fox News Digital.
OZEMPIC-STYLE DRUGS LINKED TO MAJOR SLOWDOWN IN CANCER SPREAD, NEW STUDY FINDS
There are "many lines of evidence" that suggest this would be the case, Yendamuri suggested.
"For example, when people studied patients who were having metabolic surgery to decrease obesity, for example, the incidence of cancer decreased in those patients."
While the AACR report cited studies suggesting GLP-1 medications may reduce the risk of certain cancers, it emphasized that the overall evidence is mixed and more research is needed. (iStock)
Researchers then started looking at patients who were on GLP-1 receptor agonists, such as Ozempic.

"And then they compared the incidence of cancer in those patients to patients who were not taking GLP-1 receptor agonists – and many of those studies found that the risk of cancer was lower and the survival was higher in the patients taking GLP-1s," the doctor said.
DR OZ LINKS OBESITY TO CHRONIC DISEASE SURGE, SAYS GLP-1S CAN 'JUMPSTART' BETTER HEALTH

Although the majority of studies showed this effect, Yendamuri noted that some did not identify a relationship – and a couple of studies even showed an increased risk of some specific cancers, such as thyroid cancer.

"The reason you find this disconnect … is because these are retrospective studies," he said. "That is, they look at existing data, and they're trying to derive associations from existing data … but there are many other variables that can impact the result."
The American Association for Cancer Research's 2026 Cancer Progress Report, released earlier this month, noted that obesity is a major risk factor for many cancers. (iStock)
Yendamuri and his team of researchers have conducted their own studies of the relationship between obesity and lung cancer.
"We have found in every investigation we've done that obesity does increase the risk of lung cancer," he shared.
CANCER TREATMENT DELAYS SURGE ACROSS US AS DOCTOR WARNS SYSTEM ‘NEEDS FIXING IMMEDIATELY’

Obesity also depends on how it's defined and measured, Yendamuri noted. While body mass index (BMI) has traditionally been the standard measure, many obesity researchers are moving away from relying on BMI alone and instead using more precise assessments of body fat composition.
Yendamuri shared two key findings from his research.
"If someone's having a resection, a lung cancer surgery, for patients who are on GLP-1 receptor agonists, the recurrence rate seems to be lower."
"What we think is happening is that it changes the body’s immune response to cancer cells, and thereby improves its ability to fight cancer cells."
Additionally, patients with advanced-stage cancers who are in immunotherapy and taking GLP-1s had lower recurrence rates, he noted.
Based on preclinical laboratory studies, Yendamuri said he believes GLP-1 medications have only a limited direct effect on cancer cells.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
"What we think is happening is that it changes the body’s immune response to cancer cells, and thereby improves its ability to fight cancer cells," he told Fox News Digital.
The effect may differ depending on the type of cancer, Yendamuri said, because the immune response is more important in some cancers than others.
The effect may differ depending on the type of cancer, an expert said, because the immune response is more important in some cancers than others. (iStock)
"For example, in some cancers like melanoma, we know that the immune response is incredibly important," he said.
Yendamuri acknowledged that at least some of the cancer benefit likely stems from weight loss.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"Not every patient who takes GLP-1 receptor agonists responds with a substantial weight loss, so in future trials, it would be interesting to see if the benefit for patients depends on the weight loss," he said.
"If those patients who have weight loss with GLP-1 receptor agonists have the same cancer benefit as patients who do not have weight loss, that will answer that question."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Depending on the outcomes of future trials, the doctor said he is hopeful that GLP-1 drugs could one day be regarded as a preventive mechanism for cancer.

"Not every patient who takes GLP-1 receptor agonists responds with a substantial weight loss, so in future trials, it would be interesting to see if the benefit for patients depends on the weight loss," the expert said. (iStock)

"More and more, we are realizing that apart from the treatment that you get for cancer, lifestyle modifications – exercise, decreasing weight and now GLP-1 receptor agonists – will all have a role in both enhancing the treatment of cancer as well as preventing second cancers," he said.

Yendamuri emphasized the importance of continued funding for the National Cancer Institute, noting that it supports researchers working to advance cancer research and develop new discoveries.

title: Strokes nearly double among adults under a certain age in disturbing trend
summary: Stroke incidence among young adults more than doubled over three decades, with ischemic stroke and marijuana use surging, a new study reveals.
story: Dr. Jason A. Gluck, vice chair of the Heart & Vascular Institute and system chief of cardiology at AtlantiCare in New Jersey, discusses a recent study that found stroke incidence has more than doubled among young adults.
Stroke incidence more than doubled among young adults in a recent study.
Researchers at the University of Cincinnati analyzed data from 2,076 first-ever strokes among adults ages 20–54 in the Greater Cincinnati/Northern Kentucky region from 1993-1994 to 2020.
Over those three decades, the incidence increased from about 34 to 62 strokes per 100,000 people per year.
HEART ATTACKS AND STROKES RISING WITH EXTREME WEATHER EVENTS, RESEARCH SUGGESTS
The increase was primarily driven by ischemic stroke, which occurs when a blood vessel supplying the brain becomes blocked.
Among the younger adults who experienced strokes, there was an increase in hypertension, diabetes, atrial fibrillation (irregular heartbeat) and substance use.
Stroke incidence more than doubled among young adults in a recent study. (iStock)

"This has major implications, since young people who develop disability from a stroke may no longer be able to work or provide for their families," study co-author David J. Robinson, M.D., an assistant professor of clinical neurology and rehabilitation medicine at the University of Cincinnati College of Medicine, told Fox News Digital.
"We don't know for sure why strokes are becoming more common, and we really need to study this in more depth if we are going to reverse this trend."
8 COMMON FOOD PRESERVATIVES LINKED TO HIGHER RISK OF HIGH BLOOD PRESSURE AND HEART DISEASE
There was also a sharp increase in documented substance use, which rose from 4.6% to 40.2% in the study period, primarily marijuana.

"It's hard to say whether this is responsible for any of the rise in stroke; there is a relationship between marijuana use and stroke, but most of the evidence is with heavier use," Robinson said. "The relationship between marijuana use and cardiovascular disease needs more study so that we can properly advise our patients."
The increase was primarily driven by ischemic stroke, which occurs when a blood vessel supplying the brain becomes blocked. (iStock)
In contrast to younger adults, stroke rates declined among older adults, falling from about 619 to 453 strokes per 100,000 people per year.

Short-term survival after stroke also improved, the researchers found. The share of younger adults who died within 30 days of a stroke declined from 11.7% to 9.4% – primarily for bleeding-related strokes, including intracerebral and subarachnoid hemorrhages.
WHAT TO DO IF SOMEONE IS HAVING A STROKE, AFTER JILL BIDEN REVEALED DEBATE-NIGHT FEARS

"Our study might provide evidence that we have gotten better at treating people who have hemorrhagic strokes and helping them survive, which is encouraging," said Robinson. "Still, prevention is the most important thing to focus on, because just surviving a stroke doesn't mean you aren't left without disability."
The findings were published in the journal Neurology on Sept. 23.
‘Uncommon, not zero risk’

Dr. Jason A. Gluck, vice chair of the Heart & Vascular Institute and system chief of cardiology at AtlantiCare in New Jersey, noted that while stroke is still uncommon in young adults, that doesn’t mean they have zero risk.

"The concerning findings in this particular trial is that stroke rates are moving in the wrong direction for the younger population," Gluck, who was not involved in the research, told Fox News Digital.
The share of younger adults who died within 30 days of a stroke declined from 11.7% to 9.4% – primarily for bleeding-related strokes, including intracerebral and subarachnoid hemorrhages. (iStock)
"While many of the risk factors are things that we can identify and treat before a stroke occurs, when you're young, sometimes you don't know about it – so awareness is key."
Risk factors are pervasive across all age groups, the doctor noted.
POPULAR ARTIFICIAL SWEETENER LINKED TO POTENTIALLY DANGEROUS HEART RISK

"The same things that happen to 70-year-olds can happen at 40 – if you have high blood pressure, if you have diabetes, if you’re smoking, if there's obesity, abnormal cholesterol and activity, all those things can lead to [stroke]," he warned.
"Vascular disease doesn't suddenly begin when you're 65; it develops over time."
Study limitations
The main limitation of the study is that it did not include comparable risk factors for people without stroke.

"We can't say for sure how many of the stroke risk factors are changing in people without stroke in our region," Robinson noted. "This makes it really hard to determine what is causing this rising incidence. We will need to look in other studies to really understand the ‘why’ of this trend."
"Vascular disease doesn't suddenly begin when you're 65; it develops over time," one expert said. (iStock)

Also, the findings may have been affected by changes in medical documentation and diagnostic methods over the nearly three decades. One example provided was an increase in MRI use, which could potentially improve the detection of stroke. It was also possible that the rise in substance use was due to increased documentation or disclosure.
The study was also geographically limited, including just five counties in one U.S. state.
"While stroke is still relatively uncommon in younger individuals, it can happen and be really devastating," Robinson said.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
The doctor emphasized that hypertension is the risk factor most tightly associated with stroke.
"Younger people may not have a lot of opportunities to get their blood pressure and other risk factors screened, and we need to come up with solutions that can meet them where they are," he said.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Robinson recommended using the American Heart Association’s "Life’s Essential 8," which is a checklist for optimizing your cardiovascular health.

"It includes blood pressure control along with eating better, being less sedentary, quitting any tobacco products, sleeping well, managing your weight, controlling cholesterol and managing blood sugar."
The increase was primarily driven by ischemic stroke, which occurs when a blood vessel supplying the brain becomes blocked. (iStock)
Gluck recommends using the "BE FAST" guide to determine whether someone may be having a stroke, as follows.

"If you're having these symptoms or your loved one is having these symptoms, don't drive yourself to the hospital," he advised. "Call 911. Be fast."

title: People are ditching their vapes only to pick up another surprising habit
summary: E-cigarettes promised a clean off-ramp from smoking, but severe vape withdrawal is pushing former smokers back to traditional cigarettes, experts warn.
story: High-potency nicotine, constant puffing and difficult withdrawal can make vaping hard to quit. Addiction experts explain why some users return to cigarettes—and how treating dependence may help break the cycle.
E-cigarettes have long been used as an alternative to traditional smoking, but public health data suggests some adults trying to quit vaping are turning back to cigarettes.

Recent data from Action on Smoking and Health (ASH) shows that some smokers and dual users who stop vaping opt for traditional tobacco products instead, a shift that addiction specialists say may be driven by nicotine dependence and the challenges of withdrawal.

Trent Carter, a board-certified nurse practitioner and CEO of Renew Health — a behavioral and mental health practice based in New Mexico — said that while the shift from vapes back to cigarettes might seem counterintuitive, there are behavioral reasons some users make the switch.
SINGLE WORKOUT CUTS CRAVINGS, OFFERING NEW HOPE FOR SMOKERS TRYING TO QUIT
"Vaping can become constant throughout the day, whereas a cigarette is more of a defined episode," Carter told Fox News Digital.
Public health data reveals that nearly 30% of adults who quit vaping end up returning to traditional combustible cigarettes. (iStock)

"Subconsciously, you may not even realize that you’re constantly vaping throughout the day, whereas cigarettes you feel like you're more in control because you have to think about it. You [have] to go outside, you [have] to light it up."
Unlike cigarettes, vaping can be done throughout the day and often indoors. That easy access can lead to more nicotine use and reinforce the hand-to-mouth habit, according to the expert.
High potency, severe withdrawal

E-cigarettes can be highly addictive because of the way they deliver nicotine. Many vaping devices use highly concentrated nicotine salts, allowing users to inhale large doses with each puff compared to traditional cigarettes.
"If you're consuming a large amount with every single puff ... it's going to be harder to stop when compared to a lower dose," Carter said.
SHARON STONE'S TERRIFYING WEED WITHDRAWAL SPARKS WARNING ABOUT TODAY'S POTENT MARIJUANA
Nicotine dependence alters brain chemistry by stimulating neurotransmitters like dopamine that govern mood and pleasure, according to Cleveland Clinic.
When someone abruptly cuts off high-volume intake, it can trigger rapid withdrawal symptoms, ranging from intense cravings and irritability to severe sleep disturbances and brain fog.
Unlike cigarettes, which enforce defined breaks outdoors, continuous indoor vaping tends to boost daily nicotine intake, the expert said. (REUTERS/Elijah Nouvelage)
Because high-potency vapes drive up physical tolerance, standard quitting aids — like over-the-counter patches or nicotine gum — can sometimes feel inadequate to a user seeking immediate relief.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

"While a patch or gum could definitely help with the nicotine cravings, if you're not addressing the behavioral aspect of it, then you're really falling short," Carter said. "You're leaving a huge component of why they may be smoking — whether it's because of anxiety or even insomnia during the day."
False sense of security

When e-cigarettes first hit the market, early public messaging framed them as a healthier, doctor-approved alternative to smoking, which gave many consumers a false sense of security about how difficult it would be to drop the habit, according to Carter.
Modern e-cigarettes deliver large doses of nicotine salts per puff, driving up physical tolerance and causing severe withdrawal symptoms during quit attempts. (iStock)
"If you're being told something is safe or doctor-approved, we tend to feel we're making the right choice," Carter said.

"While traditional cigarettes have toxins that e-cigarettes do not, if your daily consumption of nicotine becomes much higher, we find ourselves in a nasty cycle. You got rid of the toxins, but now you're consuming much more nicotine."
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

The elevated chemical intake carries a physical and mental toll, Carter cautioned. Heavy, uninterrupted nicotine ingestion can trigger blood pressure spikes, elevated heart rates, sleep disruption and heightened anxiety.
Breaking the dependency loop
For people trying to quit vaping, health providers warn that switching to cigarettes reintroduces harmful toxins, tar and carbon monoxide.
Addiction specialists emphasize that lasting recovery requires treating underlying behavioral triggers under professional supervision. (iStock)
Instead of switching between vaping and cigarettes, addiction specialists recommend medically supervised strategies that combine behavioral therapy with gradual nicotine reduction.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"The goal shouldn't be to find another way to consume nicotine," Carter said. "The goal should be to treat the dependence itself."
"It's not trading one for the other, but finding the underlying cause and addressing that head-on — that's how someone truly takes steps in the right direction."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

For those struggling to exit the cycle, Carter advises building self-awareness and immediately consulting a licensed addiction or mental health professional who can recommend a personalized recovery plan.
